svg.aria-label: Diagram: how Network Connectivity Center replaces pairwise peering with a global hub whose spokes get any-to-any connectivity, so it is the transitive answer to the previous post; why it replaces peering rather than layering on it, since two spokes cannot also be peered and a spoke can never export the peering subnet routes it imported, leaving any peered non-spoke network an island; the filter asymmetry where a VPC spoke controls what it exports but imports everything from its spoke group; the star topology that deliberately leaves edge spokes unconnected to each other; why auto mode networks cannot be spokes at all and the conversion to custom mode cannot be undone; and the dynamic route quota that counts destinations only and drops routes by destination when exceeded
svg.title: Network Connectivity Center: a transitive hub that replaces peering rather than layering on it
svg.text: This is the transitive answer to #81 — and it replaces peering rather than building on it.
Any network you reach by peering instead of by spoke stays invisible to the whole hub.
A global hub, and the connectivity #81 could not give you
The hub is a GLOBAL resource holding spokes from MULTIPLE REGIONS, across projects and
across organizations. Spoke types: VPC, producer VPC, NCC Gateway, hybrid.
With VPC and hybrid spokes together, ANY-TO-ANY connectivity is supported across all of
them. Latency and throughput are VM-to-VM equivalent, same as peering.
One hub per VPC spoke at a time. Site-to-site data transfer forces one shared VPC network.
It is a REPLACEMENT for peering, not a layer above it
A VPC spoke CANNOT EXPORT the peering subnet routes it imported from elsewhere. Nor can
it export policy-based, static or dynamic routes. Only its own subnet routes go to the hub.
And two VPC spokes on one hub may NOT also be peered to each other. A peered network that
is not itself a spoke is allowed — and remains unreachable from every other spoke.
So #81’s islands do not become reachable by adding a hub. They have to become spokes.
You choose what you send. You do not choose what you receive.
VPC spokes support EXPORT FILTERS ONLY — include ranges and exclude ranges — which is more
control than peering offers on the way out.
But a VPC spoke IMPORTS ALL ROUTES from its spoke group. There is no import filter, so
joining a hub accepts whatever every other spoke decided to publish.
Hybrid spokes do get import filters, and can re-advertise imported subnet routes.
Star topology puts non-transitivity back, deliberately
Two preset topologies: MESH and STAR. Mesh connects every spoke to every other.
In STAR, NCC DOES NOT CONNECT SPOKES IN THE EDGE GROUP TO EACH OTHER — which is why
peering BETWEEN two edge spokes is permitted there and nowhere else.
The exception tells you the rule: the ban on peering spokes exists to stop two paths.
Auto mode closes a second door, and this time the fix is one-way
AUTO MODE VPC NETWORKS ARE NOT SUPPORTED AS VPC SPOKES AT ALL. Not a collision risk as in
#81 — a flat refusal.
You can convert auto mode to custom mode to qualify. AFTER THE NETWORK IS UPDATED YOU
CANNOT UNDO THIS ACTION. #62’s convenient default, billed twice now, the second time one-way.
Three operational edges worth diarising
QUOTA: dynamic routes per hub are counted BY DESTINATION ONLY, ignoring priority and next
hop — and when you exceed it NCC DROPS ROUTES BY DESTINATION. Over-quota is an outage.
COOL-DOWN: moving a VPC network’s spoke to a DIFFERENT hub needs at least 10 minutes, or
the new configuration might not take effect. Re-adding to the SAME hub needs no wait.
GOVERNANCE: a same-project spoke joins immediately; a cross-project spoke becomes a PROPOSAL
a hub administrator must approve. Shared VPC networks can be spokes; grant spokeAdmin.
